title: High Schoolers Run Real Physics Experiment at CERN
summary:
Imagine designing an experiment that could help scientists understand the universe — and then actually getting to run it at CERN, the world's largest particle physics laboratory. That's exactly what six high school students from India did this spring.

The team, calling themselves attoPION, won the 13th annual Beamline for Schools competition, beating a record 712 teams from 89 countries. Their prize: two weeks at CERN in Geneva to turn their proposal into a real experiment.

But they didn't do it alone. They reached out to Manu Srivastava, a PhD student at MIT studying quantum gravity, who became their mentor. Srivastava usually declines such requests, but this one felt different. 'This email seemed very genuine,' he said. 'They wanted to do something nice and they just needed some guidance.'

The students' experiment focuses on pion charge exchange — a process where a positively charged pion interacts with a neutron to produce a neutral pion and a proton. This rare interaction is relevant to DUNE, the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, which studies neutrinos. Understanding how pions interact with matter helps researchers improve their measurements of neutrino properties.

Dave Newbold, DUNE's co-spokesperson, praised the students' proposal as 'real experimental particle physics,' not just a classroom demonstration. If successful, their work could lead to a publishable result.

At CERN, the students worked hands-on with detectors and data-acquisition systems, collected and analyzed data, and attended talks by scientists. They also had to confront the reality that the process they're studying is extremely rare, forcing them to think carefully about detection.

Berare Göktürk, a support scientist, emphasized the importance of humility: 'We prepare in the best way possible, but we also stay humble and we are aware of the limitations we have.' Her goal is for students to 'understand the journey of a scientist.'

For Srivastava, mentoring these students has been a rewarding experience that took him beyond his own field. He credits MIT's culture for encouraging him to explore questions beyond his research.

This story shows that with determination and a little guidance, young people can contribute to cutting-edge science.
why_it_matters: This matters because it shows that access to real science is not limited by age; if more teenagers get such opportunities, they could grow into the researchers who design future experiments about the universe. It also highlights the collaborative nature of science, where a small student team, a PhD mentor, and a global laboratory can work together.

background_read: CERN (the European Organization for Nuclear Research) is the world's largest particle physics laboratory, located near Geneva and straddling the French-Swiss border; its giant accelerators smash particles together to reveal how the universe is built at its smallest scale.

Beamline for Schools is an annual competition run by CERN that gives winning high-school teams a rare chance to use a real particle beamline, with scientists helping them turn a proposal into a genuine experiment.

This year's winning team, attoPION from India, focused on pion charge exchange, a rare interaction relevant to DUNE — an international neutrino experiment designed to study some of the lightest, hardest-to-catch particles in the universe.
Manu Srivastava, a PhD student at MIT (a U.S. university known for science and technology), became their mentor, helping them refine the idea and later joining them for two weeks on-site.

For high school students, operating detectors and analyzing real data at CERN is a far cry from classroom science; it also requires humility, because the process they picked is so rare they had to think hard about whether their detectors would catch it at all.

perspectives.description: The students got what almost no other high schoolers do: hands-on time with CERN's real instruments and expert mentors. Their work could even end up published, which would be a remarkable scientific achievement for a student team.

Only a tiny number of teams can win a slot at CERN, so most students will never have this experience. Even the winners had to confront how difficult and rare their process really is — a reminder that real research is slow, uncertain, and humbling.

The story fits a broader pattern of science outreach: laboratories around the world use competitions to find talent and make their work more public. High-school students can propose experiments, but the actual work still depends heavily on professional scientists and large facilities.
If the experiment succeeds, attoPION may produce a published measurement that helps DUNE. That could encourage CERN and other labs to open more beam time to young people in the future.
